title: Why stone-ground atta is different from roller-mill flour
excerpt: Heat, speed, and what gets left on the mill floor — a plain-language look at why chakki atta behaves (and nourishes) differently.
author: Meera Sharma

content.text: If you grew up watching dough rest under a damp cloth, you already know atta is not a commodity. It is a living flour. The difference between a millstone and a roller mill is not nostalgia — it is temperature, extraction, and time.
What a chakki actually does

Two circular stones turn slowly. Grain is drawn into the eye of the mill and crushed, not sliced. Because the stones run cool — typically under 60°C in our mill — the wheat germ’s oils are not scorched. Bran stays with the endosperm. You get the whole grain in the bag.
What a roller mill is designed to do

Modern roller mills are engineering marvels for shelf life. Steel rollers spin fast, generate heat, and are set up to separate bran and germ from the white endosperm. That white fraction becomes maida. Some of the bran may be added back later as ‘atta’, but the germ — where much of the flavour and vitamin E live — is often removed because its oil shortens warehouse life.

items: Chakki: whole grain, cool grind, shorter shelf life, fuller flavour.
Roller mill: high speed, higher heat, longer shelf life, milder taste.
Nutrients are not ‘added back’ as well as they are simply never taken out.

content.text: Our millers still joke that good atta should smell faintly of the field, not of a factory.

That shorter shelf life is not a flaw. It is a sign the oils are still there. Store chakki atta in an airtight tin, in a cool cupboard, and finish it within 45–60 days. Your rotis will tell you if you waited too long.

title: A quiet recipe for soft phulkas, passed down
excerpt: Water temperature, rest, and a hot tawa — the three things that matter more than any gadget.
author: Kamala Devi

content.text: There is no secret spice in a good phulka. There is flour that still has its germ, water that is not ice-cold, and the patience to let gluten and bran drink.
For 8–10 phulkas

items: About ¾ cup warm water (not hot)
½ teaspoon ghee, optional, in the dough
A pinch of salt, if you like

content.text: Method

Add water a splash at a time and knead for a full five minutes, until the dough is smooth and just tacky. Cover with a bowl and rest 20–30 minutes. Divide, roll from the centre out, and cook on a properly hot tawa — the first side until pale spots, the second until it wants to balloon. Finish on the flame if you wish, then a whisper of ghee.
If the dough fights the belan, it needed more rest, not more force.
Stone-ground atta drinks a little more water than roller-milled flour. That is the bran doing its work. Do not be shy with the water, and do not skip the rest.

title: How to store chakki atta so it stays sweet
excerpt: Because we do not strip the germ, this flour is alive. Here is how to keep it that way.
author: Bharatiya Chakki mill kitchen

content.text: Roller-milled atta is built for warehouses. Ours is not. The same oils that make rotis fragrant will turn if they sit in heat, humidity, or an open bag.
The simple rules

items: Decant into a clean, dry, airtight tin or glass jar the day the courier arrives.
Keep it away from the stove and the window. A cool cupboard is enough; refrigeration is optional in Indian summers.
Use a dry scoop. Wet spoons are how pantry moths and clumps begin.
Finish 1 kg within four to six weeks; 5 kg packs are happiest if you split them with a neighbour or freeze half.
If it smells sour or of paint, do not cook with it — write to us. Our freshness guarantee covers a replacement.

content.text: In Jaipur summers we often freeze a 5 kg pack in two zip bags. Thaw a bag overnight on the counter, still sealed, so condensation stays outside the flour.

title: Millet flours in a weekday kitchen
excerpt: Jowar, bajra and ragi are not a diet trend at our mill. They are the other half of the Indian thali.
author: Dr. Ananya Rao, consulting nutritionist

content.text: If wheat is the everyday grain of the north, millets are the climate-wise grains of the plateau and the desert. Stone-grinding them is not a flourish — millet germ is delicate, and a hot mill makes bitter flour.
Three easy ways to begin

items: Blend 20% jowar or ragi into your regular atta for a week. The dough will need a little more water and a longer rest.
Bajra shines in winter: a thick roti with ghee, or a savoury raab with buttermilk.
Ragi porridge with a date or two is a quieter breakfast than it sounds.

content.text: Because these flours are gluten-free on their own, they will not balloon like a phulka. That is not a failure. Bhakri, dosa, and porridge are their native forms — and they are excellent at them.
Diversity on the plate is older than any superfood label. A mill that only sells wheat is only telling half the story.

title: The Shekhawati wheat we mill, and the families who grow it
excerpt: A short sourcing story from the farms that have filled our chakki since the 1990s.
author: Raghav Sharma

content.text: We do not buy wheat from a commodity ticker. We buy it from people whose fathers sold grain to our father. That sounds like marketing until you have stood in a Sikar courtyard in April, watching the last of the harvest dry on a charpai.
One harvest at a time

Shekhawati wheat is not the highest-yielding grain in India. It is a hard, slightly sweet berry that holds up to millstones. We contract acreage before sowing, pay a premium for grain that is cleaned of stones and smut, and mill it in lots you can trace to a cluster of villages — not to a silo the size of a railway yard.

Organic lots from a smaller circle of farms are kept in a separate godown and milled on dedicated days. That is less efficient. It is also the only way the word ‘organic’ means anything in a bag of atta.
A mill is only as honest as its grain store.
